idea: Wilson Bentley's snowflake photomicrograph (Vermont, 1880s-1930s, public domain), halftone, captioned 'He photographed more than 5,000. Checked each one.' Appeals to people who love patient obsession and the quiet fact that nobody had ever pictured a snowflake before him.

The oldest known photograph of a tornado (28 August 1884, near Howard, South Dakota, NOAA archive) as a halftone funnel over a flat horizon, captioned 'Oldest known photograph of a tornado. 1884.' A weather nerd's flex that feels like a found document.

A Library of Congress photograph of the 1900 Galveston hurricane wreckage, captioned 'Galveston, 1900. The storm had no name, only a count.' A sober shirt for people who think about how we name and count disasters; the deadliest US natural disaster.

An early photograph of lightning from the 1880s (William Jennings, Philadelphia, public domain) printed as a white bolt on black, captioned 'One of the first lightning photographs. Taken 1882, exposure: hope.' For people who like the first time anything was seen.

A halftone of a towering cumulonimbus from the NOAA photo library, captioned 'Named in 1802 by a pharmacist.' Luke Howard gave clouds cirrus, cumulus and stratus; the shirt is for cloud-watchers and anyone who loves a good naming story.

The Black Sunday dust storm rolling over Stratford, Texas (14 April 1935, NOAA/FSA archive) as a dark halftone wall, captioned 'April 14, 1935. Somebody's topsoil.' A hard-edged environmental point of view with no slogan fluff.

A Johnstown Flood 1889 Library of Congress aftermath photograph (wrecked houses piled at the stone bridge), captioned 'The dam was known to be a problem.' A dry, pointed shirt for people who read about infrastructure and warnings ignored.

The Mount Washington Observatory in rime ice (public domain archive photo), captioned '231 mph. April 12, 1934. The record stood until 1996.' The wind record was only broken by a cyclone gust on Barrow Island; a number-with-a-story shirt.

A USGS historic photograph of a hydrographer wading or cable-gauging a river, captioned 'Somebody has to stand in the river and measure it.' Referencing the stream gauges begun in 1889 at Embudo, New Mexico; a salute to the unglamorous people behind every flood warning.

A US Weather Bureau kite being launched, 1890s (public domain), captioned 'Forecasting, 1898: fly a thermometer on a kite.' The Bureau really ran kite stations to measure upper air; charming for people who like how funny and inventive early science was.

An aerial or Library of Congress photograph of the Ohio meeting the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois, captioned 'Where two rivers stop being two.' Simple, geographic and quietly poetic for river people.

A photograph of Charles Hatfield's rainmaking tower near San Diego, 1916 (public domain), captioned 'Hired to make it rain. It did.' Floods followed, dams failed and he was never paid; a wry shirt about overpromising and getting exactly what you asked for.

The Niagara Falls ice bridge, early 1900s Library of Congress photo, with tiny figures on the ice, captioned 'Niagara ice bridge. Closed 1912.' After three people died when it broke up in February 1912, walking on it was banned; a cold, vivid image about confidence in thin things.

A Library of Congress halftone of snowbound New York streets during the Blizzard of March 1888, captioned 'March 1888. The wires came down and the city went quiet.' For people who like that one rare day the world stops.

A public-domain portrait photograph of Admiral Robert FitzRoy, captioned 'He coined the word forecast. 1860.' Mocked at the time for it; a shirt for anyone who has ever been right about the weather and blamed for it.

A USGS aerial photograph of a Mississippi River oxbow lake cut off from the channel, captioned 'The river doesn't move. It leaves.' A meander study printed as black ink on white, for people who like landscapes that are memories of water.

A historic photograph of noctilucent clouds (first photographed in 1887 by Otto Jesse in Berlin, public domain) in white on black, captioned 'Clouds at the edge of space. First noticed after Krakatoa.' Strange, true and beautiful.

The record hailstone from Vivian, South Dakota (NOAA photo, 2010) held in a hand, captioned '8 inches. 1.94 pounds. Vivian, South Dakota.' An absurd-scale weather fact that people wear to start conversations.

A Library of Congress photograph of the 1927 Mississippi flood, a levee town under water with rooftops showing, captioned 'The river was only going home.' A point-of-view shirt about land that rivers remember.

A NOAA archive photograph of a huge storm sea seen from a ship's deck, captioned 'Force 12. Beaufort wrote the scale in 1805.' For sailors and number lovers; the Beaufort scale ranks wind by what it does to the sea.
